institutionName: Institut d'Etudes Politique de Lyon (Sciences Po)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The language learning opportunity, the size of the city/amount of students, closeness to other interesting cities, access to interesting courses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. The hardest part was probably to make sure that all papers and descriptions were in check both with the home University and with the receiving university

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: well, there were a great team of international coordinators at Science Po who must have answered a ton of emails!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It's a different system with grades, evaluation form, course election etc. But overall this was communicated fairly well

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It's expensive! A good way is to ask former students already in the end of a semester whether you might be able to take their spot somewhere. If you are an avid French Learner I found it to be very nice and giving to stay with a host-family. But there are a lot of options and even affordable airbnbs

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's nice! It holds another 'local' feel to it - it feels more like a home, depending on the type of housing. Possibly, you come about more native speakers rather than if you lived with international students mostly but most campus dormitories are housing both French and international students and it should also be a unique experience. Find great people and then it's not really an issue where you'll stay!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: 3, mostly because I've met a great deal of people 'falling out of' contracts with their landlord, the amount of scams are quite high and then the price..

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I did a START course where everyone was introduced to the school at one big welcome meeting in late August. At the same time we were granted our student cards and informed on the important days and deadlines for sports activities, cafeteria, the international student organisation at the school and of course our courses

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The International student/mobility office on 2nd floor in the Science Po building was available at a decent amount of hours.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: It's very different from home and the deadline for making the final decision on whether you want a course of not is usually mid September. You are given a week or so to try different courses out before you choose and even after they no that international students might need to do some changes when coordinating the requirements of their home university with the French way.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Don't stress when it comes to figure everything out the first week or even the first month. The French system is quite laissez-faire and some course descriptions might not drop before mid term.

Also, just ask your fellow students ( and the WhatsApp chat), your professors and international coordinators about anything. really!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think this was mostly due to my courses being taught in English. I had a few very interesting ones that I really really liked and then a couple that were quite horrible to be frank. The learning outcome might have been alright in the end. It was just the enthusiasm of both students and teachers were off and some were online and probably the worst online class experience I've had so far!  Looking back at it, I'd might had wanted to change more of my courses but then again I needed do stay within a certain English-speaking diploma because of my French levels. If you dare (regardless of level) try out a course in French - and do a French speaking course on the side - it's really nice!

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: When it came to the day to day lessons I would argue that the level was lower than what I'm used to. However the evaluation could be tough and often required more detailed knowledge and exact facts that I'm used to. I'll say it was also a part of the learning experience to observe the different culture of academia and I found the switch quite refreshing really. In the end it's like at home - you get back what you give.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Less bigger lectures. More smaller classes. More group work and presentations from week to week. You were kept engaged throughout the semester.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Discourse on Borders, walls, nation and security. The Politics of Covid. EU Nuclear Independence. The politics of European Sanctions. Global Justice: an EU Perspective. Cities and aspects of globalization (additionally, a French speaking course 2h/week)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The Borders course was truly amazing! Massimiliano is a extraordinary gust professor from Torino and I loved all of the classes - he's both really passionate and professional! If you like Foucault - this one is the most post-structuralist course they offer in English at least :))

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Lost my passport. That's expensive when abroad - not recommended! Buying the wrong kind of ticket at the main station the first couple of time is a classic. Getting a subscription to their city bike system 'VeloV' is such a great idea! The city is very accessible on bike - and if you are a copenhagener you have the skills to manage the traffic in Lyon

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and housing is fairly expensive. Public transport and some trains were quite cheap!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The offer free classes at the sister university, Lyon 2 - where you can attend anything from Badminton, Dance, Self Defence, Yoga (there's a long list). You just drop by one of the first times and tell them that you're an exchange from Science Po and that's usually enoguh to register

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are many after school clubs at science po to engage in. Band, Musical, community kitchen, different Fora. Besides that, the city is very much alive with Jazz Clubs, food festivals, cinema festival, Lights festival and a new event of the big place Bellecour every weekend. You just need one insider or local to tell you all the good spots.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Jazz Club ' Hot club Lyon - super authentic, intimate setting and the jazz plus wine combination is a whole mood. Go to a few close by cities for hiking - especially around Saint Etienne there are some great mountain views. Cinemas, restaurants (Lyon is a gastronomical capital of France). A weekend- or day-trip to Annecy  cause the lake and the mountain view is out of this world pretty! Make a tradition with other students! We had a pub quiz at Wallace Bar every Monday and it was the best way to start off a new week!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Annecy, Saint tropez, Paris, Perrouges, saint-malo, Bourdeaux and Toulouse

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, it's France after all. It's a really good idea to speak the language or to learn at least some basics and then use them. They will not judge you as harshly if you at least try.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Again, language! Also, have lunch with them - lunch is a big deal and usually is a couple of hours event.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Though I didn't experience this much personally - there is still some sexist remarks from people on the street. If you can and it's daylight - call them out on it or let is pass. Also, saying high to people that you meet on stairs, elevators in classrooms are just the rule. It's super rude to ignore people on your way. Danes are not the best at this so we can probably learn a trick or two #bekindplease

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The French frankness. It seems to me that the French in general are less shy when it comes to conflict and announcing when something is wrong/intolerable. It really is refreshing to hit these issues right on (maybe instead of raging of Social Media later) they talk about things more openly and are not so afraid of admitting that the opinion they held a couple of minutes ago might not be the only version of the truth. I really like this part!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Take it easy and enjoy that you probably don't get every part of the French society and university system right away. See it as an opportunity to embrace a bit of chaos and work on your feet. It's a part of the exchange to face sudden challenges and changes as long as these don't stop you from doing exciting things, you'll be glad for them in the end. Make room in your budget for pivoting, sudden changes, spontaneous trips etc. And give yourself a rest day to catch up with yourself, deadlines, the mobility platform when you loose your sense of clarity.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people! I miss them so much !

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Housing, making sure I was living up the the Erasmus requirements and getting all my ECTS in check. Pre-approval can be quite tought when they don't really do course descriptions before really late in France...

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
